analysis.one_liner: Directs Medicare to negotiate drug prices with manufacturers and use the savings to shrink the coverage gap.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: introduced in September 2007 with 10 cosponsors from both parties, it died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare's Part D drug benefit has a hole in coverage (often called the 'donut hole'): after beneficiary and plan spending reach a yearly limit, seniors pay the full cost of their drugs out of pocket. This bill would repeal the law that bars the government from interfering with drug price negotiations and instead direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices with drug manufacturers, the way other federal agencies that buy drugs in bulk can. Every dollar of savings would be used to raise the coverage limit, shrinking the donut hole starting in 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors with high annual prescription drug costs, who currently fall into the donut hole and pay full price for their medications, would get more covered spending each year. Medicare as a program would pay less per drug through negotiated contracts. The bill was written so that savings and expanded coverage roughly offset each other on the government's books.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'noninterference' provision of Medicare Part D and authorizes the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate contracts with drug manufacturers, with authority similar to other federal agencies that buy drugs in bulk.
Requires the Secretary to negotiate prices for each fallback prescription drug plan and to join negotiations for any covered drug at a plan's request.
Redirects every estimated dollar of savings from negotiated prices into raising the initial coverage limit beginning in 2009, so the donut hole shrinks by roughly the amount Medicare saves.
The bill was introduced by Senator Bill Nelson with five original cosponsors including Republican Susan Collins, and drew 10 cosponsors overall (9 Democrats, 1 Republican).

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would receive lower prices from Medicare's negotiator than they currently get from Part D plans, which today negotiate separately and are barred from government negotiation. Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers could face a new, larger bargaining counterparty across the market. The bill deliberately forbids the Secretary from imposing a particular formulary or price structure, so plans would continue to operate and compete.

drawbacks.text: The bill forbids the Secretary from imposing a particular formulary or price structure, which removes the main lever other federal negotiators use. Critics of similar proposals argued that negotiation without formulary control could yield little real savings.
Mandatory negotiation applies only to the fallback plans; for other plans the Secretary must act only when a plan asks, so coverage of the bargaining authority is partial rather than government-wide.

Expanding the initial coverage limit increases Medicare drug spending, which is offset only by estimated savings from negotiation; if those savings fall short, the expansion could strain the Medicare Prescription Drug Account.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors who hit the donut hole, the potential benefit is concrete and immediate: more of their drug costs covered each year. The main design weakness is that the negotiator is barred from the tools (formulary and price structure control) that produce the deepest discounts elsewhere in government purchasing, so the promised savings that fund the benefit are uncertain. On balance, the bill shifts bargaining power from drug makers toward beneficiaries at limited government cost, but a stronger version would have given the negotiator more leverage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2007, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Nelson of Florida introduced the Medicare Prescription Drug Gap Reduction Act of 2007 on September 25, 2007, with original cosponsors Whitehouse, Mikulski, Collins, Kohl, and Kerry.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day it was introduced.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearings, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call in either chamber.
The bill attracted 10 cosponsors, 9 Democrats and 1 Republican (Senator Susan Collins of Maine).
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because the bill that would have ended the ban on government price negotiation died without a vote, leaving Part D plans to pay manufacturer prices and the donut hole in place for seniors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers, and seniors left in the gap

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan in form but heavily Democratic: 9 of 10 cosponsors were Democrats, with one Republican, and the bill never reached a roll call where partisan lines could be measured.

industries.note: The bill repeals the ban on government price negotiation and requires Medicare to negotiate contracts with manufacturers, directly cutting the prices Part D pays them. Their loss is seniors' gain: the savings fund expanded drug coverage.

industries.industry: Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plans would keep running Part D and competing, but a government negotiator stepping in for fallback plans (and on request for others) would reduce their control over drug pricing. The bill is written to preserve their role rather than replace it with a government drug benefit.
Beneficiaries who fall into the coverage gap would see the initial coverage limit raised each year by the amount of the negotiated savings, meaning more of their drug costs covered starting in 2009.
